description:
Have You Ever Seen the Ghostly Glow After Sunset?

Episode 122 of a daily journey through the universe. 🌌
We hunt the zodiacal light: a faint cone of light in the west after evening twilight on moonless spring nights (late February to April in the Northern Hemisphere), sunlight scattered by dust from comets and Mars, and why you need a dark sky to see it.

➡️ Tomorrow, Episode 123: Next stop, light pollution. Why most people can't see the Milky Way anymore.
Start from Episode 1 "Leaving Earth" on the channel.
Follow so you don't miss a stop. A new episode every day.

Images: NASA (public domain)
Narration: AI voice

#space #zodiacallight #astronomy #shorts #science #nasa

segments.text: Have you ever seen a ghostly cone of light after sunset? Most people never have.
On spring evenings, after the sky gets completely dark, a faint cone of light can rise from the western horizon.
segments.headline: A cone of light

segments.text: It's the zodiacal light. Sometimes called the false dusk.
segments.headline: The false dusk

segments.text: It's sunlight, bouncing off countless grains of dust that fill the space between the planets.
segments.headline: Sunlit space dust

segments.text: In twenty twenty-one, scientists found that much of that dust might come from Mars, and from comets breaking apart.
segments.headline: Dust from comets and Mars

segments.text: It follows the same path across the sky as the Sun and planets. That's why it's named after the zodiac.
segments.headline: Along the planets' path

segments.text: In the Northern Hemisphere, the best time is now: late February to April, about an hour or two after sunset, with no Moon.
In autumn, look before dawn, in the east.
segments.headline: In autumn: before dawn

segments.text: It's brighter than the Milky Way in places, but city lights wash it out completely. You need a truly dark sky.
segments.headline: You need dark skies

segments.text: Tomorrow, the reason most people alive today have never seen the Milky Way. And it's getting worse. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
